Roadie
ROH-dee
noun (Boomer slang)
Shortened from road manager or road crew, the people who travel with a touring band to haul, set up, and run its equipment. Roadie appears in the late 1960s, as rock tours grew from a van and an amplifier into convoys of trucks, lights, and sound systems; the 1980 film Roadie and countless tour memoirs made the figure familiar. The word is now used for any behind-the-scenes helper.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A roadie is the crew member who hauls the gear, builds the stage, tunes the guitars, and tears it all down at two in the morning so the band can play the next town. No one buys a ticket to see him, and the show cannot happen without him. The Christian observation: the roadie is one of the most biblical figures in rock and roll. Scripture is full of roadies. When Israel moved through the wilderness, the sons of Kohath carried the tabernacle furnishings: "after that, the sons of Kohath shall come to bear it ... These things are the burden of the sons of Kohath" (Num 4:15). They never stood in the Holy of Holies; they carried what made worship possible. Paul says the church works the same way: "the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee ... Nay, much more those members of the body, which seem to be more feeble, are necessary" (1Co 12:21–22). The Lord of glory Himself took the roadie’s place: "For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many" (Mar 10:45). Every congregation runs on roadies — the deacon who fixes the boiler, the women who set up the fellowship meal, the man who runs the sound board and is noticed only when it fails. "Whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men" (Col 3:23). The roadie’s reward is not applause; it is "Well done, thou good and faithful servant" (Mat 25:21).

Webster 1828 Definition

Late-1960s rock slang (from road manager / road crew) for the touring crew who move and run a band’s gear — the unseen servant Scripture honors, like the sons of Kohath (Num 4:15) and the Son of man who came to minister (Mar 10:45).

ROADIE, n. (rock slang, late 1960s–) A member of a touring band’s crew who transports, sets up, and maintains its equipment; hence any behind-the-scenes helper.

Webster (1828) — ROAD, noun [Latin gradior. See Grade .] 1. An open way or public passage; ground appropriated for travel, forming a communication between one city, town or place and another. The word is generally applied to highways, and as a generic term it includes highway, street and lane. The military roads of the Romans were paved with stone, or formed of gravel or pebbles, and some of them remain to this day entire. 2. A place where ships may ride at anchor at some distance from the shore; sometimes called roadstead, that is, a place for riding, meaning at anchor.

Decode for families: in church, roadies are called deacons, volunteers, and mothers.

Modern Corruption

Rock culture made the star everything and the roadie invisible; Scripture honors the unseen servant and shows the Lord Himself taking the servant’s place.

expand to see more

The world of the 1970s rock tour was not a holy place, and the roadie’s life often included the excesses of the stars he served. But the role itself exposes a lie at the heart of celebrity culture: that the person on stage is the one who matters. Every concert is the work of dozens of unseen hands. The same lie works its way into churches, where the preacher or the worship leader can seem to be the whole show. Paul’s body imagery (1Co 12) is the cure: the hidden members are "necessary."

The gospel goes further. The greatest Person in the universe did the roadie’s work — washing feet, serving, and carrying the heaviest burden of all to a cross (Mar 10:45). A son who learns to set up chairs and stack them afterward without being thanked is learning to be like Christ.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English rád (a riding, a journey) → road → road manager / road crew → late-1960s roadie.
